previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with alcoholic cirrhosis and a history of varices, encephalopathy, and prior GI bleeds was admitted for melena and transient hypotension. She presented with black tarry stools and spitting up dark material, concerning for upper gastrointestinal bleeding. In the ED, she received dextrose for hypoglycemia, IV fluids, and one unit of packed red blood cells for volume resuscitation. Her hemoglobin stabilized, and she had no further episodes of hypotension. An EGD revealed new grade 1 esophageal varices without active bleeding and diffuse gastric erythema with a biopsy taken. Her renal function, which was initially impaired with a creatinine of 1.3, improved to baseline of 0.9 with hydration. Leukocytosis resolved without evidence of infection. She remained neurologically stable without recurrence of prior facial droop or weakness. She was discharged home with stable vital signs, instructions to follow up on biopsy results, and a short course of ciprofloxacin for infection prophylaxis, continuing her liver-directed medications and transplant evaluation.
problems: Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, with bleeding
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
